This stage uses the section header table from lesson 32 and the segment and section tables of the three formats from lesson 40 . What you build. You write five functions in the layout module: shannon_entropy(data) returns bits per byte, rounded to 4 decimal places. sections(data) lists every section with a permission string and the entropy of its bytes. segments(data) lists ELF program headers and Mach-O segments. section_at_offset(section_list, offset) and section_at_address(section_list, address) find the owner of a file offset or a virtual address. Stages 4, 5, and 6 use them. Why it matters. Sections tell you what the link editor made. Segments tell you what the loader maps and with which permissions. A section that is writable and executable, or a data section with entropy near 8, is a fact a reviewer must see before a release. Entropy measures how evenly the byte values spread. The maximum is 8 bits per byte, when all 256 values occur equally often, and zero padding is 0. In the fixtures, the code sections measure from 5.5 to 5.9 and the string sections from 4.0 to 4.7. The padding between segments measures 0.0. Compressed or encrypted data comes close to 8. Each format stores permissions in a different place: Format Where Bits ELF section sh_flags SHF_WRITE 0x1 , SHF_ALLOC 0x2 , SHF_EXECINSTR 0x4 ELF segment p_flags PF_X 0x1 , PF_W 0x2 , PF_R 0x4 COFF and PE section Characteristics MEM_EXECUTE 0x20000000 , MEM_READ 0x40000000 , MEM_WRITE 0x80000000 Mach-O segment initprot , maxprot VM_PROT_READ 1 , VM_PROT_WRITE 2 , VM_PROT_EXECUTE 4 An ELF section without SHF_ALLOC is not loaded, so its string is "---" . A Mach-O section has no permission bits of its own. It takes initprot of the segment with the same name. In a Mach-O object the only segment has an empty name, so use the instruction attributes ( 0x80000400 ) for "r-x" and the table MACHO_SEGMENT_PERMS for the rest. Work through one concrete case. Its size is 4, but it holds no bytes in the file. So file_size is 0 and its entropy is 0.0. Now compute entropy for the 15-byte string tally report v3 . On the arm64 executable, __TEXT,__text is 768 bytes with entropy 5.8595, __TEXT,__cstring is 4.6413, and __DATA,__common is zerofill with file_size 0. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_02.py (135 lines) Copy See it drawn Entropy in bits per byte Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Entropy measures how unpredictable the bytes are, from 0 (all identical) to 8 (every byte value equally likely). Zero padding scores 0, this repetitive text about 3, and random bytes about 7.2: close to the maximum of 8, which only very long random inputs reach, since 256 bytes cannot contain all 256 values evenly. Compiled code usually lands around 5 to 6.5, and compressed or encrypted data near 8, which is why a high-entropy section in an ordinary program is worth a second look. You write three functions in the symbols module: read_cstring(data, offset, end=None) reads one NUL-terminated name and refuses a name that has no terminator before end . demangle(name) turns a supported Itanium C++ name into its source form, or returns None . symbols(data) returns every symbol of the file in one shape. Why it matters. Symbols are the names a reviewer reads first: which functions a build defines, which ones it needs from elsewhere, and what strip removed. All three formats store names as offsets into a string table. A name offset that points outside its table is the most common corruption in a damaged file. A reader that does not check it prints text from some other table. Why it matters. The bytes of a call or a pointer in an object file are often zero. The relocation record says what the link editor writes there. In a linked image, the loader fills import slots before the program runs. On current macOS, the fixup information sits inside the pointer slots themselves, as chained 64-bit words. A disassembler that reads one of those slots without decoding it reports a pointer to an address that does not exist. Lesson 20.40 opens with that exact mistake. Solutions Solution Refusing unsupported formats Parsing them with assumptions made for little-endian 64-bit files would produce plausible but wrong numbers. A clear refusal tells the user what to do (extract one architecture first) instead of misleading them. Solution Prologues at -O2 Optimizing compilers skip frame setup in small leaf functions and interleave instructions, so the familiar "save registers, set frame pointer" pattern is often missing. At -O0 nearly every function has it. Solution A new dependency New imports (library and symbol names), likely growth in __text and __stubs , new strings, and new function starts, each listed in the diff with sizes. Solution B1 · An unchecked size Python would silently return a short slice (or a huge allocation in other languages), and later code would misread it as the section's content. a2049: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects Exploring Decision Tradeoffs Lesson 20.49 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Declare options and evidence Compute comparable scores Explore sensitivity and dominance Export the chosen scenario Before you start Needs : nothing beyond the earlier phases. Type : Project, level 3 (). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : TypeScript. In plain words first The idea in one line Show when a different priority changes the preferred option. The problem In plain words first A weighted scoring table ("accessibility 50 %, setup time 30 %, visitor flow 20 %") makes a decision look objective. It can hide three things: an option whose data is missing, a hard limit one option breaks, and how close the result is, so that a small change in priorities flips the winner. This project builds a decision board that shows all three. Options and criteria are declared with fixed ranges and a source note for every value. Scores are normalized honestly, with missing values and broken limits making an option ineligible rather than quietly scoring zero. A sensitivity sweep shows when changing one weight reverses the ranking. The board exports the chosen scenario as a reusable decision record. Help a community team compare practical project options using a user-supplied criteria table and supporting notes. Apply explicit constraints, weighted scores and sensitivity analysis, keep missing values visible, and export an interactive HTML decision board and a reusable decision record. Standard libraries only. Four stages, approximately eight hours. TypeScript implementations are exercised by the grader. What you will build: An interactive tradeoff board, criteria.csv and decision-record.json Step 1 · Declare options and evidence Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · TypeScript Make ranges, constraints and uncertainty explicit. What you build. Create a table of criteria and options. Every criterion declares a fixed min/max range, cost or benefit direction and a nonnegative weight. Every option supplies a numeric value or null plus a source note for every criterion. Null means not measured, never zero. Worked example. Open gallery has access 9, setup 8 and flow 8. Exhibition pods has 6,2,7. The archive layout has unknown flow and stays visible but ineligible. All three fixtures are authored teaching data. Implement the contract. parse(text:string):Decision . Criteria: {id,label,weight,direction,min,max,limit?} . Options: {id,label,values:{criterion:number|null},notes:{criterion:string}} . Reject duplicate IDs, missing notes, out-of-range numbers, unknown criterion keys and zero or nonfinite total weight and nonfinite range widths. At most 30 criteria, 200 options and one MiB. Reject malformed input before producing a partial artifact. The tests include held-out records separate from the demonstration fixture. Checks The checks this stage must pass: stage.test.ts (74 lines) Copy Step 2 · Compute comparable scores Step 2 of 4 · about 2 hours · TypeScript Normalize units without hiding missing values or hard constraints. What you build. Benefit normalization is (value-min)/(max-min); cost normalization is (max-value)/(max-min). Normalize the active weights to sum to one. A cost limit is a maximum; a benefit limit is a minimum. Any missing value or limit violation makes the aggregate score null. Worked example. Open gallery normalizes to access .9, setup .2, flow .8. At weights .5,.3,.2 the score is .67. Pods scores .68 and ranks first. An unknown archive flow produces null rather than a renormalized score. Implement the contract. normalize(c:Criterion,v:number):number ; score(data,weights={}):Row[] sorted by descending score then ID. A row has {id,label,score,missing,violations,normalized} . Weight overrides are raw nonnegative magnitudes; invalid, overflowed or all-zero weights throw. Read weight overrides only from own properties; criterion IDs such as constructor are valid data. Checks The checks this stage must pass: stage.test.ts (80 lines) Copy Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ For a cost criterion such as setup hours, a lower value normalizes to a higher score. ✗ An option with a missing value can be scored as 0 on that criterion. That penalizes "unknown" as if it were "worst"; the option is ineligible until measured. ✓ Ranges are fixed in advance, so adding an irrelevant option cannot change the others' scores. ✗ A higher weighted score means the option is objectively better. In plain words first The idea in one line Turn workload events into a timeline with the exact objects behind each clue. The problem In plain words first When a Kubernetes rollout goes wrong, the clues are events: "Failed", "BackOff", "Started", repeated dozens of times across pods with generated names. Reading raw event lists is slow, and asking an assistant to read them risks leaking configuration and drawing conclusions from event reasons alone. This project turns exported events and workloads into a timeline. Go parses the export while keeping when each event happened separate from when the export was taken, merges repeated snapshots of the same event, connects each event to the workload revision that produced the pod by following owner references (never by guessing from names), and exports a redacted context pack. TypeScript renders the timeline from that pack. Help an on-call engineer inspect exported Kubernetes events and workload snapshots. Group repeated events, distinguish observation time from occurrence time, and link each suggested investigation to object identity and rollout revision. Export an HTML timeline and a redacted JSON context pack for an assistant. Standard libraries only. Four stages, approximately eight hours. Go, TypeScript implementations are exercised by the grader. a2052: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects An LLM Gateway with Fallbacks Lesson 20.52 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Validate provider endpoints Classify failures without retrying everything Send one bounded HTTP request Route with a total-attempt budget Before you start Needs : Structured outputs Type : Project, level 3 (Engineer). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Go. In plain words first The idea in one line Route a bounded request through providers with explicit failure semantics. The problem In plain words first Calling one model provider is a single point of failure. A gateway that falls back to a second provider helps, if it knows when to fall back. Retrying a rate limit (429) or a server error (5xx) on another provider makes sense. Retrying a malformed request (400) everywhere just multiplies the failure. Following a redirect could send your API key somewhere you never configured. This project builds a small HTTP gateway in Go with explicit failure rules: validated provider URLs, a status classifier with three outcomes, one bounded attempt (size and time limits, no redirects), and a router that walks providers in order under a total attempt budget and one overall deadline, keeping each provider's credentials to itself. Build a local non-streaming HTTP proxy with real provider fallback, per-provider environment credentials, response limits, and one overall deadline. Verify the complete wire path with loopback servers. Go 1.22 or later, standard library only. Four stages, about eight hours. You need structs, slices, callbacks, errors and basic JSON; the stage prerequisites link to the relevant curriculum. Start with the offline example before connecting a provider. Where it stops: Connect an existing chat-completions client to a local fallback endpoint Trace provider outages without forwarding caller credentials Step 1 · Validate provider endpoints Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · Go Treat the provider list as trusted configuration. What you build. Implement Endpoints(values) before opening a connection. Allow HTTPS, plus HTTP on exactly localhost , 127.0.0.1 or ::1 for local services. Reject userinfo, fragments, queries, line breaks, missing hosts and other schemes. Remove exact duplicates while preserving provider order. In plain words first The idea in one line Build a content-addressed document index with deletion tracking, version checks, and freshness-aware retrieval. The problem In plain words first A RAG system answers from an index of documents. a2057: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects Retry Storms: a Lab Lesson 20.57 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Model concurrent failures with a deterministic clock Compare bounded backoff and jitter Enforce shared retry budgets and server delays Replay against a local HTTP service Before you start Needs : nothing beyond the earlier phases. Type : Project, level 3 (). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Go, TypeScript. In plain words first The idea in one line Watch many reasonable retries combine into an overloaded service. The problem In plain words first One client retrying a failed request is sensible. Twenty clients retrying the same overloaded service at the same moment is a retry storm: each retry adds load exactly when the service can least take it, and a short outage turns into a long one. This project makes the storm visible. A deterministic replay simulates many clients against a failing service on a virtual clock. Bounded exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries out. A shared retry budget caps the total number of retries across clients, and server hints such as Retry-After are honoured. Finally the same policy runs against a local HTTP service, and the counters are checked independently. Help SDK authors choose retry behavior when many clients fail together. Replay concurrent clients against a deterministic service model, compare bounded backoff and jitter with a shared retry budget, then run the same policy against a local HTTP fixture. Export amplification and recovery timelines with a reusable client policy. Standard libraries only. Four stages, approximately eight hours. Go, TypeScript implementations are exercised by the grader. What you build. Replay clients that all begin at time zero. The service returns 503 before failUntil or when the count at the exact millisecond exceeds capacity. Sort scheduled attempts by time then client ID. Success ends that client. The supplied fixed Delay scaffold supports this stage; richer backoff comes next. Worked example. Three clients, capacity 2 and failUntil=0 produce two initial successes and one 503. With one allowed attempt, the report has three calls and two successes. Initial calls are never counted as retries. Implement the contract. Replay(clients,failUntil,capacity int,p Policy,budget int)(Report,error) . Policy fields are BaseMS, MaxMS, Attempts, Jitter, Seed. Version-1 report has mode, clients, calls, successes, retries and timeline. Limits: 0..1000 clients, 1..10 attempts, positive capacity, nonnegative time and budget. Reject malformed input before producing a partial artifact. The tests include held-out records separate from the demonstration fixture. What you build. Backoff before retry n starts at BaseMS and doubles until MaxMS. Jitter selects a deterministic integer in [0,cap] from the client, attempt and seed. This arithmetic sequence is an educational reproducibility device, not a cryptographic random generator. Worked example. Base 10 and cap 25 produce 10,20,25,25 without jitter. With jitter enabled, each client can schedule a different delay. A zero delay is valid full jitter and may amplify the same time bucket. Implement the contract. Delay(p Policy,client,attempt int) int , with attempt numbered from 1 for the first retry wait. Mix ((client+1) 1103515245 + attempt 12345 + seed) using uint64: xor with x>>16, multiply by 2246822519, xor with x>>13, then take modulo (cap+1). Validate rejects invalid bounds. With "full jitter" (a random wait between 0 and the backoff), the same 60 retries spread across dozens of windows and the busiest holds only a few. The seed is per client, so the run is reproducible; real conclusions need several seeds, as the exercises say. Step 3 · Enforce shared retry budgets and server delays Step 3 of 4 · about 2 hours · Go Bound aggregate attempts across clients, not just each individual request. What you build. Add a shared cap on scheduled retries to Replay. A mutex-protected Budget uses Take to admit at most the declared number across live goroutines. Parse Retry-After as nonnegative integer seconds or an HTTP date. A past HTTP date yields zero delay. Worked example. Twenty clients may each allow four attempts, but a shared budget of 12 bounds the simulation at 32 total calls. Admission is deterministic by schedule order in simulation and depends on goroutine order in live mode. Implement the contract. NewBudget(n int)*Budget ; (*Budget).Take()bool ; ServerDelay(value string,now time.Time)(time.Duration,error) . Invalid values fail. A live server delay above MaxMS stops the request rather than retrying earlier than instructed. It limits one process; a fleet needs a shared admission service. In plain words first The idea in one line Reconnect a streamed answer without duplicating text or hiding an incomplete result. The problem In plain words first Chat answers arrive as a stream, token by token. Connections drop. This project builds stream recovery for server-sent events (SSE). It decodes bytes incrementally so characters and events survive any chunk boundary, applies events by stable id so a repeated event changes nothing, reconnects with the id of the last accepted event, keeps a cancelled answer as a draft, and exports a trace that can rebuild the answer exactly. A tool contract specifies required parameters, property types, and validation keywords like enum , minimum , and maximum . A valid call provides the required parameters matching their declared types. The problem In plain words first Agent jobs (write a report, summarize an incident) take time, and workers crash. The problem In plain words first Most requests are fast, but a few are very slow, and in a system that makes many calls, those few dominate how slow it feels. Hedging is a classic remedy: if the first request has not answered after a short delay, send a second copy to another replica and take whichever answers first. It works, and it costs extra requests. This project measures both sides. It summarizes latency with nearest-rank percentiles, launches a duplicate only when the delay expires, lets only a valid response win (a fast error is not a winner), records the losing request even after cancellation, and exports latency and extra work side by side. The problem In plain words first "Run the agent's code in a sandbox" covers a wide ladder of protections: a separate process, a restricted filesystem, a container with its own network rules, a micro virtual machine with its own kernel. a2073: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects An Inbox for Signed Webhooks Lesson 20.73 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Preserve raw bytes and delivery identity Verify signatures and timestamp bounds Deduplicate retries with a durable inbox Replay accepted deliveries with processing receipts Before you start Needs : nothing beyond the earlier phases. Type : Project, level 4 (). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Go. In plain words first The idea in one line Accept a delivery once and retain the evidence needed to replay it safely. The problem In plain words first Services tell each other about events through webhooks: an HTTP POST saying "this report was uploaded". The receiver must check that the POST really came from the sender (a signature), that it is not an old message replayed by someone else (a timestamp window), and that a retry of the same delivery is processed once. And when processing has a bug, you want to replay accepted deliveries later, deliberately, without re-accepting them as new. This project builds such a receiver in Go: it keeps the raw request bytes, verifies an HMAC signature over the delivery id, timestamp and body, stores each accepted delivery durably before acknowledging it, answers retries as duplicates, and replays stored deliveries through an explicit command that writes processing receipts. Help developers feed external events into an agent workflow without losing retries or accepting altered payloads. Verify an authored signature scheme over the raw body, enforce timestamp bounds, and store stable delivery identities before dispatch. Export an HTTP receiver and a replay CLI that distinguishes a transport retry from a new business event. Standard libraries only. Four stages, approximately eight hours. Go implementations are exercised by the grader. What you will build: Local webhook receiver, delivery ledger and explicit replay CLI Step 1 · Preserve raw bytes and delivery identity Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · Go Read the exact authenticated body before decoding business data. What you build. Read POST requests with X-Delivery-ID, X-Timestamp and X-Signature. Preserve raw bytes exactly. JSON whitespace is part of the signed content; decoding then reserializing would alter the authenticated message. Worked example. The fixture body ends with a newline on disk. Signing that file includes its newline. Removing the final byte changes the signature even though the JSON object represents the same data. The transport delivery ID is distinct from business eventId inside the body. Implement the contract. ReadDelivery(*http.Request)(Delivery,error) returns ID, Timestamp, Signature, Body. Require POST, canonical int64 decimal timestamp, ID matching [A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,127}, and 1..65536 raw bytes. JSON validity is a processing-stage concern. Reject malformed input before producing a partial artifact. The tests include held-out records separate from the demonstration fixture. Checks The checks this stage must pass: stage_test.go (52 lines) Copy Step 2 · Verify signatures and timestamp bounds Step 2 of 4 · about 2 hours · Go Authenticate identity, timestamp and raw bytes under an explicit teaching scheme. What you build. The authored signature is v1= followed by lowercase HMAC-SHA256 hex over decimalTimestamp + dot + deliveryID + dot + rawBody. The shared secret comes from an environment variable and is never written to the inbox. Verify with hmac.Equal and bound accepted timestamps. Worked example. At now=1770000000 and a 300-second window, now-300 and now+300 are accepted. now-301 is stale. Altering a single body byte or delivery ID fails authentication even inside the time window. Implement the contract. Sign(key []byte,id string,timestamp int64,body []byte)string ; Verify(Delivery,key,now,skew)error . Keys require at least 16 bytes; skew must be 0..1 hour. Receiver uses five minutes. This format is original and not compatible with a named webhook provider. Parsing the JSON and serializing it again produces the same data with different whitespace, and the signature no longer matches. That is why the receiver keeps and verifies the raw bytes before decoding anything. compare_digest compares in constant time, so the check does not leak how many characters matched. Step 3 · Deduplicate retries with a durable inbox Step 3 of 4 · about 2 hours · Go Persist accepted identity and body before acknowledging delivery. What you build. Write a mode-0600 temporary file, sync its content, and publish it through an atomic no-overwrite hard link. Sync the directory before acknowledging success. Delivery filenames are SHA-256 digests of IDs, preventing path traversal. Existing IDs with identical raw bytes are transport retries; changed bytes are conflicts. Worked example. The first signed delivery returns HTTP 202. The same ID and bytes return 200 without replacing the original acceptedAt. The same ID with a newly valid signature but a different body returns 409. A changed body under the old signature returns 401 before storage. Implement the contract. Accept(dir,id,body,now)(Entry,created,error) ; LoadEntry(dir,id)(Entry,error) . Entry stores schemaVersion, deliveryId, base64 body, sha256 and acceptedAt. ErrConflict identifies reused delivery IDs. Corrupt stored records fail closed. Replay starts a new, explicitly named processing run; transport deduplication is unchanged. Step 4 · Replay accepted deliveries with processing receipts Step 4 of 4 · about 2 hours · Go Make a new processing run explicit while keeping transport deduplication intact. What you build. Replay reads only accepted inbox entries. The authored local processor extracts eventId and data from JSON and writes a processing receipt keyed by delivery ID plus explicit run ID. Repeating the same run returns its existing receipt; a different run is a deliberate replay. Worked example. Delivery delivery-1 carries business-42. Replay run review-1 creates one receipt; repeating review-1 creates none. A new delivery-2 may carry business-42 and is a distinct transport identity. Business-level deduplication is a downstream policy. Implement the contract. Replay(dir,id,run,now)(Processing,created,error) ; fields schemaVersion, deliveryId, runId, businessEventId, bodySHA256, processedAt and payload. The first replay under run id review-1 created a processing receipt (with the body's SHA-256, the business event id and the payload); the second replay with the same run id did not ( sameRunCreatedAgain: false ). One receipt in total, and nothing about the transport side changed. Read the finished code The complete reference, file by file. Exercises Send the same JSON with different whitespace and compare its raw SHA-256 digest. Do not use semantic JSON equality at the signature boundary. (step 1) Add a provider adapter only after implementing and testing its published raw-byte signing rules. Do not assume a different service uses this concatenation order. Go HMAC and Go SHA-256 . (step 2) Kill a process between writing and linking. Unlinked .pending files can remain but are never accepted deliveries. This local-filesystem design requires hard-link and fsync support; do not claim equivalent behavior on arbitrary network filesystems. (step 3) Feed receipt.payload to a downstream queue with an idempotency key. External exactly-once effects require a separate transactional design; a local processing receipt cannot establish that guarantee. (step 4) Solutions Solution Whitespace and digests The raw SHA-256 changes with any whitespace change, even though the JSON means the same. Signatures are over bytes, so the receiver must hash and verify the bytes it received, never a re-serialization. Solution Another provider's scheme Each provider defines its own concatenation, header names and encoding. Implement its published rules exactly, with its test vectors, in a separate adapter; reusing this scheme would reject all their real deliveries, or worse, accept forged ones. Solution A crash before linking The .pending file stays on disk, but only linked entries count as accepted deliveries. The sender's retry is then accepted normally. The design relies on hard links and fsync, so it should not be claimed for filesystems without them. Solution Downstream effects Send receipt.payload to the next queue with the run id plus delivery id as the idempotency key. Exactly-once effects in other systems still need those systems to honour the key; a local receipt cannot guarantee it. Solution B1 · Re-serializing before verifying Preserve and verify the raw bytes first. Any change to how JSON is written changes the bytes, so verifying a re-serialization fails legitimate deliveries. a2074: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects A Streaming Agent Shell in Rust Lesson 20.74 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Parse a deliberately small action language Confine file tools to a bounded root Track budgets and terminal state Stream bounded JSON events through real stdin Before you start Needs : Data management , Tool schema design Type : Project, level 4 (Systems). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Rust. In plain words first The idea in one line Build a real stdin/stdout Rust action loop with bounded reads, an explicit command grammar, path containment, and streamed JSON events. The problem In plain words first Coding agents need to look at a repository: list files, read one, search for a string. Giving them a real shell does that and much more, which is the problem. This project builds a tiny observation shell in Rust that any agent can drive over stdin and stdout, and that can do only what it says. It parses a deliberately small command language (help, pwd, list, read, literal search, quit) and rejects everything else, shell syntax included. File tools resolve paths inside one root and refuse anything that escapes it. Every request uses one slot of a budget, and quit is final. Input lines are size-limited before they are read, and every reply is a JSON event with a sequence number and the request's id. An inspectable repository-observation process usable by different coding agents. The Rust process accepts a deliberately small tool language. Its Python adapter accepts JSONL with caller ids and tool arguments, then translates only known commands. No argument becomes an operating-system shell command. Where it stops: JSONL requests use caller ids and explicit tool argument objects. Step 1 · Parse a deliberately small action language Step 1 of 4 · about 2 hours · Rust Define an action enum for help, pwd, list, read, literal search and quit. Unknown commands are rejected, including shell-like instructions. Search separates its pattern and path with a tab so spaces remain valid inside either argument. a2077: Course home / Phase 20 · Hands-On AI Projects Coordinating a Distributed Eval Farm Lesson 20.77 480 min Project Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Partition stable case identities Fence each shard lease Accept idempotent completion receipts Run a bounded local worker pool Before you start Needs : Go 1.22 or later on Linux or macOS, Python 3.10 or later for the grader, Go structs, pointers, errors and JSON files, Goroutines, channels and context cancellation Type : Project, level 5 (Frontier). Time : about 8 hours over 4 steps. Code in : Go. In plain words first The idea in one line Partition cases, lease shards and aggregate bounded concurrent workers. The problem In plain words first A large evaluation is split across many workers. Some crash mid-run, some are slow and finish after their work was given to someone else. The final score must still count each test case exactly once, from the right result. This project coordinates an evaluation farm in Go. Cases are assigned to shards by a stable hash of their ids, so a restart knows which cases belong where. A shard is leased with a version that survives process death, and a new worker advances that version (fencing) when it takes over. A result is accepted only from the current lease, once. Finally a pool of real worker processes runs the farm, with a crash injected to prove recovery. Turn a file of recorded model predictions into a resumable evaluation run. Separate worker processes acquire persisted shards, compare answers and publish fenced receipts. Kill a worker after its claim, restart the run and prove an old worker cannot overwrite the replacement's result. Go fits the coordinator because the same dependency-free binary can launch child workers, bound concurrency and coordinate filesystem state. This implementation distributes work across processes on one Linux or macOS host. It does not provide a multi-machine transport or perform model inference. Four stages take about 8 hours. Solutions Solution Hashing ids Chunks depend on file order and length: adding or reordering one case moves many others to different shards, which breaks resumption. A hash of each id gives a placement that never changes for that case. Solution A repeatedly failing shard Count attempts per shard and stop retrying after a limit, marking it failed with the last error. Retrying forever hides a case that crashes every worker. Solution Several machines Replace the local file lease with a shared coordinator that supports compare-and-swap (a database row, etcd, or similar), keep the same versioned fencing, and store receipts there too. Solution B1 · Double-counted shard The second result for shard 7: only one receipt per shard is accepted, and only from the current lease version. In plain words first The idea in one line A decompiler for a defined x86-64 subset that turns functions in an object you compiled into structured C, then proves the output. The problem In plain words first A decompiler turns machine code back into readable source. Commercial tools do it for whole programs; this project does it for a handful of small C functions compiled to x86-64, entirely from scratch in Python, and then proves its output is right. It is the deepest build in the course and follows phase 13's reverse-engineering lessons step by step: read the ELF object and its relocations; decode the instructions the fixtures use; recover control flow, including a jump table; lift to an intermediate form and SSA; simplify compiler idioms (such as division by a constant done with multiplication); recover the function signature and types; structure the graph into if, while and switch; and finally recompile the emitted C and check it matches the original byte for byte, with relocations masked. A decompiler for a defined x86-64 subset. It reads an ELF relocatable object that you compiled, turns each function into structured C, and then proves the output: it recompiles the C, compares relocation-masked bytes, runs the original and the decompiled version side by side over an input grid, and writes an evidence report that lists every unknown. The core uses the Python standard library only. clang is optional: it enables the recompile and differential legs of stage 8. The grader checks your selected workspace; it never fills in missing behavior from the reference. Analyze only programs that you compiled from source. The fixtures are small C functions written for this project. What you will build: A decompiler that turns the functions of an x86-64 relocatable object you compiled into one C file, and an evidence report that says what was proved and what stays unknown. Where it stops: Run python3 -m minidec verify on your own object and its source. The command writes decompiled.c, recompiled.o and report.json; a CI job can fail on status fail or unknown. Step 1 · Read an ELF relocatable object Step 1 of 8 · about 2 hours · Python Validate the ELF64 header, read section headers, the symbol table and every RELA record, and cut each function out of .text with its relocations and its alignment padding. A PC-relative record points at S + A + (end of instruction - P), so a target is resolved only with the end of the instruction that holds the field. Read the project prerequisites first. This stage applies An ELF Binary Reader from Scratch: Program Anatomy and the relocation part of Disassembly and Control Flow . What you build. You build the loader that every later stage reads from. It accepts the bytes of one ELF64 little-endian x86-64 relocatable object ( ET_REL ), and it gives back: the section headers, each with its name and its bytes, the symbol table, with name, value, size, type, binding and section name, every RELA record, grouped by the section it patches and sorted by offset, one function at a time: its bytes, the relocations inside it, and the alignment padding after it. It also resolves a relocation to the place it points at after linking. Why it matters. A relocatable object is the output of clang -c . The link editor has not run yet, so every address that refers to another section is a field of zero bytes plus a RELA record. The jump table of band , the lookup table at -O1 , and every call to another function are visible only through those records. If the loader drops them, stage 3 cannot find the jump table, stage 7 cannot name the lookup table, and stage 8 compares bytes that the link editor will overwrite. A function symbol gives the start and the size. The bytes between the end of one function and the start of the next are alignment padding. Stage 3 decodes the padding with a linear sweep to show where the sweep and the recursive descent disagree, so the loader reports it separately. Work through one concrete case. Build the fixture yourself, or use the committed objects. The objects were built with: Copy The header of samples-x86_64-O1.o starts with 7f 45 4c 46 02 01 : the magic, ELFCLASS64 (2) and little-endian (1). At offset 16, e_type is 1 ( ET_REL ) and e_machine is 62 ( EM_X86_64 ). The section header table is at e_shoff , each entry is 64 bytes, and the first five section names are the empty null section, .strtab , .text , .rela.text and .rodata . .text is 0xb2 bytes long. The five function symbols, in address order, with their sizes: name value size next start padding tenths_and_fifths 0x0 0x23 0x30 13 thirds 0x30 0x1a 0x50 6 band 0x50 0x17 0x70 9 fold 0x70 0x26 0xa0 10 record 0xa0 0x12 0xb2 0 band holds one relocation. The record in .rela.text has r_offset 0x5f, type 2 ( R_X86_64_PC32 ), the .rodata section symbol, and addend -4. Inside the function the offset is 0x5f - 0x50 = 0xf. The field belongs to leaq (%rip), %rcx , which starts at 0x5c and ends at 0x63. The psABI says the link editor stores S + A - P in a PC-relative field, where S is the symbol value, A is the addend and P is the field address. The processor adds the field to the address of the next instruction. So the operand reaches: Copy The table starts at .rodata+0x0 . Its first eight bytes are 05 00 00 00 08 00 00 00 : the values 5 and 8 of the switch in band . At -O0 , .rodata itself has six relocations, one per jump table entry. Each is a PC-relative record against .text whose target, resolved with the table base as the end, is 0x78, 0x81, 0x8a, 0x93, 0x9c and 0xa5. These are the six case blocks of band . Change the addend, the field offset and the instruction length in the lab. The target moves by the same amount as the distance from the field to the end of the instruction, which is why relocation_target refuses a PC-relative record without that end. Implement the contract. Read every section header; SHT_NOBITS has no bytes. Name sections from e_shstrndx . Then set self.symbols and self.relocations . Any table outside the file raises ElfError . ElfObject._read_symbols() -> list[Symbol] Every 24-byte Elf64_Sym of every SHT_SYMTAB , named through the string table at sh_link . Type is st_info & 0xf , binding is st_info >> 4 . ElfObject._read_relocations() -> dict[str, list[Relocation]] Every 24-byte Elf64_Rela of every SHT_RELA , keyed by the name of section sh_info , sorted by offset. A symbol index past the table raises ElfError . ElfObject.function_extent(name, section=".text") -> (start, end, padding_end) From the function symbol: start is the value, end is start + size , padding_end is the next function start or the section size. Unknown names raise ElfError . ElfObject.function(name, section=".text") -> FunctionBytes The bytes in [start, end) and the relocations inside that range, with offsets relative to start . relocation_target(relocation, field_end=None) -> Target Absolute: S + A . PC-relative ( R_X86_64_PC32 , R_X86_64_PLT32 ): S + A + (field_end - P) . A PC-relative record with no field_end raises ValueError . A section symbol has S = 0. The CLI is supplied. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_01.py (115 lines) Copy Step 2 · Decode the x86-64 subset Step 2 of 8 · about 3 hours · Python Decode legacy prefixes, REX, one and two byte opcodes, ModRM, SIB, displacements and immediates for the instructions the fixtures use. Record where the displacement and immediate fields sit so relocations can be matched to operands. Every instruction must agree with the captured disassembler listing by address, bytes and AT&T text. This stage applies Disassembly and Control Flow , sections "The Instruction Format Has One Rule Per Field" and "Linear Sweep". What you build. You build a decoder for the part of x86-64 that clang emits for the fixtures at -O0 and -O1 . decode(code, address) reads one instruction and returns an Instruction with its bytes, a normalized operation, its operands, its operand width, its control-flow kind and its branch target. It also records where the displacement field and the immediate field sit inside the instruction. linear_sweep decodes a byte range in address order and lists every byte that it cannot decode. The decoder is checked against a disassembler listing. For every instruction of the four committed objects, your address, your bytes and your AT&T text must equal the captured listing. Why it matters. Every later stage trusts the decoder. A wrong operand width changes a 32-bit value into a 64-bit value, and the recompiled C then differs from the original. A wrong field offset makes stage 3 miss the relocation on the lea that holds the jump table base. The listing gives you an oracle with no judgment in it. You do not decide that your decode looks right. You compare it. Checks The checks this stage must pass: test_stage_02.py (144 lines) Copy Step 3 · Recover control flow Step 3 of 8 · about 2 hours · Python Follow control flow by recursive descent, resolve the position-independent jump table from its relocations and bounds check, split basic blocks, then compute dominators, dominance frontiers, post-dominators, back edges and natural loops. An indirect jump with no matching idiom stays unresolved and is reported. This stage applies Disassembly and Control Flow , sections "Recursive Descent", "Basic Blocks", "Dominators With the Iterative Algorithm" and "The Jump Table in grade at -O0", and Compiler Idioms and Optimization for the bounds-check idiom. What you build. You build the control-flow graph of one function: recursive_descent decodes only the bytes that control flow reaches from the entry. A jump table resolver turns jmpq *%rax into a list of targets, with the table found through its relocation and its length taken from the bounds check. ControlFlowGraph splits the instructions into basic blocks with typed edges: jump , taken , fallthrough and table . The graph computes reverse postorder, immediate dominators, dominance frontiers, post-dominators, back edges and natural loops. Why it matters. A linear sweep decodes alignment padding as if it were code. Recursive descent decodes only what can run, but it stops at an indirect jump unless something tells it where the jump goes. For the fixtures that something is the relocation on the lea that loads the table base and the relocations inside the table. Dominators are the input of everything after this stage. SSA places phis on dominance frontiers (stage 4). A back edge is an edge to a block that dominates its source, and every loop that stage 7 emits starts from one. The immediate post-dominator of a branch is the place where its two arms join again, and stage 7 uses it to close an if . Work through one concrete case. band at -O0 occupies 0x50 to 0xba, with 6 bytes of padding up to 0xc0. Without a resolver, recursive descent from 0x50 decodes 16 instructions. It follows the ja at 0x62 to the default block at 0xae, falls through to 0x64, and stops at jmpq *%rax at 0x76. That jump is listed in unresolved , and the six case blocks are never reached. What you build. You build two things. The lifter turns each decoded instruction into IR statements. The IR has assignments, stores, branches, jumps, a switch through a recovered table and returns. Its expressions are constants, variables with a width, binary operations, casts, loads, flag records and section addresses. Registers become variables named by their 64-bit family ( eax writes rax at width 32). The flags register is an ordinary variable named flags . Frame bookkeeping ( push , pop , mov %rsp, %rbp , stack adjustments) produces no statements, and a slot at a constant offset from %rbp becomes a local variable such as local_8 . The SSA builder gives every definition its own version. It places phi statements on the iterated dominance frontier of each variable's definition sites, renames uses over the dominator tree, and inserts a cast where a use has a different width than the definition it reads. Why it matters. x86-64 instructions do several things at once. subl %edi, %esi writes %esi and six flags. A later jle reads two of those flags. SSA makes every later question local. "Which value does this use read?" has one answer, the single definition with that version. What you build. You build signature recovery for the optimized SSA function: Parameters. The System V psABI passes the first six INTEGER arguments in %rdi , %rsi , %rdx , %rcx , %r8 and %r9 . A register read at version 0 is read before any write. The highest such argument register fixes the count, so a function that reads only %rsi still has two parameters. Union-find joins them, and each web gets one name: param_N for an argument, local_8 for a stack slot, eax_1 for a register value. Types. The widest definition in a web gives int or long . A web used as the base of a scaled element access becomes a pointer to the element. A web used as the base of constant offsets becomes a pointer to a struct with one field per offset. Pointer types spread along copies and phis. Signedness. Arithmetic shifts, signed division, signed compares and sign extension say signed. Logical shifts and unsigned division say unsigned. A lone unsigned compare is the range-check idiom of a switch , and it does not make the value unsigned. Return type. The width of the value in %rax at each return. If no path writes %rax , the result is void , and that guess is listed as an unknown. Every decision carries the instructions that support it. Why it matters. The machine code has no types. A wrong parameter count changes the call in the stage 8 driver. A wrong width truncates a long . A wrong signedness flips the result of a compare for negative inputs. In plain words first The idea in one line Improve an explicit routing skill from labeled development errors, then require a separate evaluation gate before promotion. The problem In plain words first "Self-improving" agents are an attractive idea and an easy way to fool yourself: an agent that edits its own rules until its test score goes up has simply learned its test. This project builds a self-improving skill with the limits that make it honest. The skill is a transparent router: an ordered list of word rules mapping support messages to a team. Labelled cases are split into development and holdout sets by a hash of their ids, with the split audited for leaks. New rules are proposed only from mistakes on the development set, and only for words that point to one label. A candidate is promoted only if it improves the untouched holdout without breaking a case that used to be right, and even then promotion waits for a person.
